Brown teal (Anas chlorotis) hatchlings emerge from eggs incubated at 39 °C [T = 39 °C] after a developmental period of approximately 28 days [ab = approximately 28 days]. This incubation duration falls within the range typical for small-bodied dabbling ducks and reflects the thermal demands of the embryonated egg stage. The mass of freshly hatched ducklings averages about 61.4 grams [Ww0 = about 61.4 grams], a value consistent with the initial wet weight reported for other members of the genus Anas. This modest neonatal mass imposes a tight energetic budget during the first days of life, as the downy chick must transition from yolk absorption to active foraging under parental guidance. The thermal environment during the egg stage, maintained at a stable 39 °C [T = 39 °C], appears critical for normal organogenesis, and deviations from this temperature can extend hatching time or reduce hatchling viability in captive breeding programs.

Once hatched, the nestling period of the Brown teal proceeds rapidly, and fledging is achieved at approximately 53 days after hatching [tx = approximately 53 days after hatching] under standard thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Field observations indicate that the attainment of first flight, or fledgling independence, typically occurs within a window of 50 to 55 days post-hatch, with the onset of flight feather maturation marking the end of the nest-dependent chick phase. During this period, the developing chick relies heavily on parental provisioning, and the timing of fledging is influenced by both food availability and the ambient temperature regime. The relatively short interval to fledging in this species, compared to some larger waterfowl, may reflect an adaptive strategy to reduce predation risk during the vulnerable pin-feathered chick stage, allowing young birds to reach safer aquatic habitats sooner.

Sexual maturation in Brown teal occurs after a protracted juvenile phase, with puberty estimated at 159 days after hatching [tp = 159 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained under thermoneutral conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This milestone, marking the onset of gonadal activity and gametogenesis onset, is not immediately followed by breeding; instead, first-year birds typically defer reproductive effort until their second year. The delay between achieving puberty and initiating reproduction is thought to reflect the time required for young individuals to acquire sufficient body condition and establish a breeding territory. Body mass data from wild populations show that adult females attain a maximum recorded body mass of 410 grams [Wwi = 410 grams], whereas adult males are substantially larger, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 521 grams [Wwi = 521 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is common among waterfowl and is linked to male-male competition for access to females during the breeding season, as larger males often have a competitive advantage in aggressive encounters.

The reproductive schedule of the Brown teal is characterized by low annual output, with females producing a single clutch of 5 to 6 eggs per nesting event [N_R_i = 5 to 6 eggs per nesting event] and raising only one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year]. This slow reproductive tempo, combined with the modest clutch size, makes the species particularly sensitive to predation pressure and habitat degradation. The first breeding attempt typically occurs at 1.5 years since birth [tR = 1.5 years since birth] under a steady ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a delay that reflects the need for juveniles to accumulate sufficient lipid stores before diverting resources toward offspring production. Nesting adults invest considerable energy in incubation and brood-rearing, and the low fecundity per annum suggests that adult survival, rather than high fecundity, is the primary demographic driver of population persistence in this endangered anatid.

Basal metabolic rate measurements in adult Brown teal have yielded a maximum oxygen consumption of 417.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 417.5 milliliters per hour] when recorded at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This resting metabolic rate is consistent with values reported for other small dabbling ducks and likely reflects the energetic cost of maintaining homeothermy in cool temperate wetlands. Longevity records from banded individuals indicate that the maximum lifespan in the wild is approximately 19.6 years [am = approximately 19.6 years], a remarkably long duration for a duck of this body size and a life-history strategy that compensates for low annual reproductive output through extended reproductive at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] opportunities. The oldest documented individual in a New Zealand population persisted for over two decades, underscoring the importance of adult survival for the species' conservation. Such a slow pace of life, with delayed maturity, small clutch sizes, and high adult survival, positions the Brown teal as an extreme example of the K-selected end of the life-history continuum among Anatidae.
